items.new: When they searched, they found that the casks most recently lowered into the hold were perfectly sound, and that the leak must be farther off. So, since the weather was calm, they broke out deeper and deeper, disturbing the slumbers of the huge ground-tier butts and sending those gigantic moles up from that black midnight into the daylight above. They went so deep, and the lowest puncheons looked so ancient, corroded and weedy, that you almost expected to find next some moldy cornerstone cask containing coins of Captain Noah, along with copies of the posted placards that vainly warned the infatuated old world about the flood. Tierce after tierce of water, and bread, and beef, too, and shooks of staves (bundled staves for making casks), and iron bundles of hoops, were hoisted out, until at last the piled decks were hard to get about on; and the hollow hull echoed underfoot, as if you were treading over empty catacombs, and reeled and rolled in the sea like a demijohn with nothing but air for freight. The ship was as top-heavy as a dinnerless student with all of Aristotle in his head. It was just as well that the Typhoons did not visit them then.

items.new: Poor Queequeg! When the ship was about half disemboweled, you should have stooped over the hatchway and peered down at him there, where, stripped to his woolen drawers, the tattooed savage was crawling about amid that dampness and slime like a green spotted lizard at the bottom of a well. And a well, or an icehouse, it somehow proved to be for him, poor pagan; for there, strange to say, for all the heat of his sweating, he caught a terrible chill which turned into a fever, and at last, after some days' suffering, laid him in his hammock, close to the very sill of the door of death. How he wasted and wasted away in those few long, lingering days, until there seemed little left of him but his frame and his tattooing. But as everything else in him thinned, and his cheekbones grew sharper, his eyes nevertheless seemed to grow fuller and fuller; they took on a strange softness of luster, and looked out at you mildly but deeply from his sickness, a wondrous testimony to that immortal health in him which could not die or be weakened. And like circles on the water, which expand as they grow fainter, his eyes seemed rounding and rounding, like the rings of Eternity. An awe that cannot be named would steal over you as you sat beside this waning savage and saw things in his face as strange as any seen by those who stood by when Zoroaster died. For whatever is truly wondrous and fearful in man has never yet been put into words or books. And the approach of Death, which levels all alike, impresses all alike with a last revelation, which only an author returned from the dead could adequately tell. So that — let us say it again — no dying Chaldee or Greek had higher and holier thoughts than those whose mysterious shadows you saw creeping over the face of poor Queequeg, as he lay quietly in his swaying hammock, and the rolling sea seemed to be gently rocking him to his final rest, and the ocean's invisible flood-tide lifted him higher and higher toward his destined heaven.

items.new: Every man in the crew gave him up for lost; and as for Queequeg himself, what he thought of his condition was forcibly shown by a curious favor he asked. He called one of the men to him in the gray morning watch, just as day was breaking, and, taking his hand, said that while in Nantucket he had happened to see certain little canoes of dark wood, like the rich war-wood of his native island; and on inquiring, he had learned that all whalemen who died in Nantucket were laid in those same dark canoes, and that the idea of being laid out that way had greatly pleased him. For it was not unlike the custom of his own people, who, after embalming a dead warrior, stretched him out in his canoe and so left him to be floated away to the starry archipelagoes; for not only do they believe that the stars are islands, but that far beyond all visible horizons their own mild, uncontinented seas flow together with the blue heavens, and so form the white breakers of the Milky Way. He added that he shuddered at the thought of being buried in his hammock, according to the usual custom at sea, tossed like something vile to the death-devouring sharks. No: he wanted a canoe like those of Nantucket, all the more congenial to him as a whaleman because, like a whaleboat, these coffin-canoes had no keel — though that meant uncertain steering, and a great deal of leeway down the dim ages.

He then called for his harpoon, had the wooden stock drawn from it, and then had the iron part placed in the coffin along with one of the paddles of his boat. Also at his own request, biscuits were then arranged round the inside walls; a flask of fresh water was placed at the head, and a small bag of woody earth scraped up in the hold at the foot; and when a piece of sailcloth had been rolled up for a pillow, Queequeg now begged to be lifted into his final bed, so that he might try out its comforts, if it had any. He lay without moving for a few minutes, then told someone to go to his bag and bring out his little god, Yojo. Then, crossing his arms on his chest with Yojo between them, he called for the coffin lid (hatch, he called it) to be placed over him. The head part turned back on a leather hinge, and there lay Queequeg in his coffin with little but his composed face in view. "Rarmai" (it will do; it is easy), he murmured at last, and signaled to be put back in his hammock.

He spent many spare hours carving the lid with all kinds of grotesque figures and drawings; and it seemed that in this way he was trying, in his rough fashion, to copy parts of the twisted tattooing on his body. And this tattooing had been the work of a departed prophet and seer of his island, who, by those hieroglyphic marks, had written out on his body a complete theory of the heavens and the earth, and a mystical treatise on the art of attaining truth; so that Queequeg in his own proper person was a riddle to unfold, a wondrous work in one volume, but one whose mysteries not even he himself could read, though his own living heart beat against them; and these mysteries were therefore destined in the end to molder away with the living parchment on which they were inscribed, and so remain unsolved to the last. And it must have been this thought that prompted Ahab's wild exclamation when, one morning, he turned away from surveying poor Queequeg — "Oh, devilish tantalization of the gods!"

items.new: To any meditative Magian rover, this serene Pacific, once seen, must forever after be the sea of his adoption. It rolls the midmost waters of the world, the Indian Ocean and the Atlantic being only its arms. The same waves wash the breakwaters of the newly built Californian towns, planted only yesterday by the most recent race of men, and bathe the faded but still gorgeous skirts of Asiatic lands older than Abraham; while between them all float milky ways of coral islands, and low-lying, endless, unknown archipelagoes, and impenetrable Japans. Thus this mysterious, divine Pacific girdles the world's whole bulk; makes all coasts one bay to it; seems the tide-beating heart of the earth. Lifted by those eternal swells, you cannot help but acknowledge the seductive god, bowing your head to Pan.

items.new: Taking advantage of the mild, summer-cool weather that now reigned in these latitudes, and in preparation for the especially active pursuits expected shortly, Perth, the begrimed, blistered old blacksmith, had not moved his portable forge back to the hold after finishing his share of the work on Ahab's leg, but kept it on deck, lashed fast to ringbolts by the foremast; for he was now almost constantly called on by the headsmen, and harpooners, and bowsmen to do some little job for them — altering, or repairing, or reshaping their various weapons and boat gear. Often he would be surrounded by an eager circle, all waiting to be served, holding boat-spades, pike-heads, harpoons and lances, and jealously watching his every sooty movement as he toiled. Nevertheless, this old man's was a patient hammer wielded by a patient arm. No murmur, no impatience, no petulance came from him. Silent, slow and solemn, bowing his chronically broken back still further, he toiled away as if toil were life itself, and the heavy beating of his hammer the heavy beating of his heart. And so it was. — Most miserable!

items.new: He was an old man who, at the age of nearly sixty, had belatedly encountered that thing called, in the technical language of sorrow, ruin. He had been a craftsman of famed excellence, with plenty to do; he owned a house and garden, embraced a youthful, daughter-like, loving wife and three merry, rosy-cheeked children, and every Sunday went to a cheerful-looking church planted in a grove. But one night, under cover of darkness, and further concealed in a most cunning disguise, a desperate burglar slid into his happy home and robbed them all of everything. And darker still to tell, it was the blacksmith himself who unknowingly led this burglar into the heart of his family. It was the Bottle Conjuror! When that fatal cork was drawn, out flew the fiend and shriveled up his home. Now, for prudent, most wise and economical reasons, the blacksmith's shop was in the basement of his house, but with a separate entrance of its own; so the young, loving, healthy wife had always listened — with no unhappy nervousness, but with vigorous pleasure — to the stout ringing of her young-armed old husband's hammer, whose echoes, muffled by passing through the floors and walls, came up to her, not unsweetly, in her nursery; and so, to stout Labor's iron lullaby, the blacksmith's infants were rocked to sleep.

items.new: Oh, grassy glades! Oh, ever-vernal endless landscapes in the soul; in you, though long parched by the dead drought of the earthy life, in you, men yet may roll like young horses in new morning clover; and for some few fleeting moments feel the cool dew of the life immortal on them. Would to God these blessed calms would last. But the mingled, mingling threads of life are woven by warp and woof: calms crossed by storms, a storm for every calm. There is no steady unretracing progress in this life; we do not advance through fixed gradations, and at the last one pause — through infancy's unconscious spell, boyhood's thoughtless faith, adolescence's doubt (the common doom), then skepticism, then disbelief, resting at last in manhood's pondering repose of If. But once gone through, we trace the round again; and are infants, boys, and men, and Ifs eternally. Where lies the final harbor, from which we unmoor no more? In what rapt ether sails the world, of which the weariest will never weary? Where is the foundling's father hidden? Our souls are like those orphans whose unwedded mothers die in bearing them: the secret of our paternity lies in their grave, and we must go there to learn it.

Not only had barrels of beef and bread been given away to make room for the far more valuable sperm, but additional casks had been bartered for from the ships she had met; and these were stowed along the deck and in the captain's and officers' staterooms. Even the cabin table itself had been knocked into kindling; and the cabin mess dined off the broad head of an oil-butt, lashed down to the floor for a centerpiece. In the forecastle, the sailors had actually caulked and pitched their chests and filled them; it was humorously added that the cook had clapped a head on his largest boiler and filled it; that the steward had plugged his spare coffee-pot and filled it; that the harpooners had headed the sockets of their irons and filled them; that, indeed, everything was filled with sperm except the captain's trouser pockets, and those he reserved for thrusting his hands into, in self-satisfied testimony of his entire satisfaction.

items.new: As this glad ship of good luck bore down upon the moody Pequod, the barbaric sound of enormous drums came from her forecastle; and as she drew still nearer, a crowd of her men were seen standing round her huge try-pots, which, covered with the parchment-like skin called the poke, the stomach-skin of the black fish, gave out a loud roar at every stroke of the crew's clenched hands. On the quarter-deck, the mates and harpooners were dancing with the olive-hued girls who had eloped with them from the Polynesian Isles; while, suspended in an ornamented boat firmly secured aloft between the foremast and mainmast, three Long Island negroes, with glittering fiddle-bows of whale ivory, were presiding over the hilarious jig. Meanwhile, others of the ship's company were tumultuously busy at the masonry of the try-works, from which the huge pots had been removed. You would almost have thought they were pulling down the cursed Bastille, such wild cries they raised as the now useless brick and mortar were being hurled into the sea.

items.new: Now, in that Japanese sea, the days in summer are floods of brilliance. That unblinkingly vivid Japanese sun seems the blazing focus of the glassy ocean's immeasurable burning-glass. The sky looks lacquered; there are no clouds; the horizon floats; and this nakedness of unrelieved radiance is like the unbearable splendors of God's throne. It was well that Ahab's quadrant, the instrument for measuring the sun's height, was fitted with colored glasses through which to sight that solar fire. So, swinging his seated body to the roll of the ship, and with his astrological-looking instrument to his eye, he held that posture for some moments to catch the exact instant when the sun should reach its precise meridian. Meanwhile, while his whole attention was absorbed, the Parsee was kneeling beneath him on the ship's deck, and with his face thrown up like Ahab's, was eyeing the same sun with him; only his eyelids half hooded his eyes, and his wild face was subdued to an earthly passionlessness. At length the desired observation was taken; and with his pencil on his ivory leg, Ahab soon calculated what his latitude must be at that precise instant. Then, falling into a moment's reverie, he looked up again toward the sun and murmured to himself: "You sea-mark! You high and mighty Pilot! You tell me truly where I am now — but can you cast the least hint of where I shall be? Or can you tell where some other thing besides me is living this moment? Where is Moby Dick? This instant you must be eyeing him. These eyes of mine look into the very eye that is even now beholding him; aye, and into the eye that is even now equally beholding the objects on the unknown, far side of you, you sun!"

items.new: Then, gazing at his quadrant and handling one after another its many cabalistic contrivances, he pondered again, and muttered: "Foolish toy! Babies' plaything of haughty Admirals, and Commodores, and Captains; the world brags of you, of your cunning and might; but what, after all, can you do, except tell the poor, pitiful point where you yourself happen to be on this wide planet, and the hand that holds you — no! not one jot more! You cannot tell where one drop of water or one grain of sand will be tomorrow noon; and yet with your impotence you insult the sun! Science! Curse you, you vain toy; and cursed be all the things that cast man's eyes aloft to that heaven whose live vividness only scorches him, as these old eyes are even now scorched with your light, O sun! Level by nature to this earth's horizon are the glances of man's eyes; not shot from the crown of his head, as if God had meant him to gaze on his firmament. Curse you, you quadrant!" dashing it to the deck. "No longer will I guide my earthly way by you; the level ship's compass, and the level dead-reckoning, by log and by line — it is these that shall guide me, and show me my place on the sea. Aye," leaping down from the boat to the deck, "thus I trample on you, you paltry thing that feebly points on high; thus I split and destroy you!"
